item.title: Why Are We Suckers for Pseudoscientific Personality Tests?
item.description:
Personality

Why Are We Suckers for Pseudoscientific Personality Tests?

Even unscientific personality tests feed a core human need for identity.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • We like to categorize ourselves into social identities to satisfy core social needs.
  • The MBTI is a corporate and cultural phenomenon despite being unreliable and unscientific.
  • The MBTI's biggest scientific flaw—forcing complex human traits into categories—is what makes it so popular.
  • The Big Five test is much more reliable and more accurate at predicting major life outcomes.

The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator (MBTI) is the most popular and well-known measure of personality. Fifty million people have taken the assessment and it has been used by 89% of Fortune 500 companies at some point to screen and evaluate employees, generating millions of dollars in annual revenue for the Myers-Briggs Company.

People put their Myers-Briggs category on their Tinder profiles, and several years ago funders even put up $1 million to develop an app matching couples based on their Myers-Briggs personality types. While the Myers-Briggs test is telling people who to hire and marry, scientists hate it. As Laith Al-Shawaf has noted, “Any psychologist will tell you, it’s mostly bulls**t.”

Then why is it so popular?

Primarily, it's because people are suckers for terrible psychology tests.

Let’s start with the MBTI. The test was developed during World War II by an American mother and daughter who were fascinated by Carl Jung’s 1921 book Psychological Types. They created a series of 93 questions, like, “Are you more (a) realistic than speculative or (b) speculative than realistic.”

Source: Wikipedia user Jake Beech.

After you complete the Myers-Briggs test, you get sorted into one of 16 categories. Each group is given an appealing name: the “logical pragmatist” or the “insightful visionary”—providing a perfect new title for a professional development seminar or your online dating profile.

Another perk is that you get matched with famous people. Are you an “ISFP” like Bob Dylan and Rihanna, or an “INTP” like Albert Einstein and Tina Fey?

We (Dom and Jay) both completed the test and were categorized as “Commanders” with an ENTJ personality type. This puts us in prestigious—and tyrannical—company, like Steve Jobs, Franklin D. Roosevelt, and Gordon Ramsay. (Here’s the MBTI test if you want to try it yourself.)

This is Jay’s Myers-Briggs personality profile (Dominic was the same “type”).
Source: 16 Personalities Results

Despite the joy of being compared to celebrities, psychologists have repeatedly argued that the Myers-Briggs has minimal predictive ability and is grounded in debunked theory. If you take the test more than once, it’s also quite likely to give you different answers each time.

Another big problem is that these 16 categories contradict how contemporary psychologists think about personality. Many experts posit that human personality can be boiled down to five traits—the BIG 5 of extraversion, agreeableness, conscientiousness, openness to experience, and neuroticism. Each trait is continuous, so someone can score high, low, or anywhere in between. (To take a Big 5 test yourself, follow this link.)

A report in Scientific American compared the Myers-Briggs to other personality scores, ranging from the Big 5 to Astrological signs, to see how each predicted 37 life outcomes (see their full report), ranging from how many close friends they had, to how often they exercised, to how satisfied they were with life.

Here’s what they found:

Source: Seth Stephens-Davidowitz & Spencer Greenberg, 2024

On average, the Big Five test was about twice as accurate as the MBTI-style test for predicting these life outcomes, placing the usefulness of the MBTI-style test halfway between science and astrology—literally.

Unfortunately, it is quite hard to conceive of yourself in five-dimensional space. It’s also awkward to tell people at a conference, first date, or a job interview that you have a moderate score on extraversion, moderate-to-high on agreeableness and conscientiousness, high on openness, and moderate-to-low on neuroticism. This is hardly sparkling dinner party conversation!

This is why assigning people to Myers-Briggs’ categories is compelling: People would much rather claim a social identity that includes Sun Tzu, Isaac Newton, Jane Austen and Arthur Ashe (setting aside the absurd fact that some of them were deceased hundreds of years before the test was even invented).

The use of categories is a great marketing maneuver and a big part of the reason behind the popularity of many dubious personality tests, from the Myers-Briggs to the infamous TIME magazine Harry Potter Quiz or Cosmo’s quiz to help you learn what kind of lover you are. The same logic also applies to astrology signs.

Source: Blake Johnson

All these tests operate a bit like the Sorting Hat from Harry Potter, slotting us into different groups. People crave self-definition and social identities provide this for us. We are attracted to group memberships that provide both a sense of connection to people just like us and distinction from others—what Marilynn Brewer termed “Optimal Distinctiveness.” These groups fulfill core social needs.

The ease with which people form group identities can be traced back to the minimal group experiments from the 1970s. People were randomly categorized into groups after completing a test of dubious merit, such as their ability to estimate the number of dots in an image or their preference for abstract art. Within minutes, they had created a new sense of identity and were treating their new in-group members very differently from out-group members.

When we use personality tests that impose categories—like the Myers-Briggs or astrology—we risk exaggerating differences between groups and similarities within them. When this occurs with other types of identities like race or gender, we typically call it “stereotyping” and we try to avoid it. When consultants do it in companies, they are exploiting the same social psychology to make a buck.

This is why organizations could do much better by creating other meaningful social identities to create a sense of belonging.It is also why you should focus less on fictitious identities—like whether you are a Commander or an Aries—and more on real ones that matter. And if you do want to make romantic decisions based on personality, we highly recommend using a scientifically valid personality test like the Big 5.

To get a weekly email with insights into the science of identity, subscribe to The Power of Us Newsletter. You can also dive deeper by picking up a copy of The Power of Us book or explore research from the NYU Center for Conflict and Cooperation.

item.title: In Law Enforcement, Everything Old Is Not Really New Again
item.description:
Law and Crime

In Law Enforcement, Everything Old Is Not Really New Again

The psychology of older ideas in modern contexts.

Posted August 6, 2026

Key points
  • As forensically relevant situations change, law enforcement must change with them.
  • Yet, as in many walks of life, this doesn't necessarily happen.
  • Well-documented military situations can show us the psychology of such failures to adapt.
Source: Matthew Sharps

Society and law enforcement face increasingly and frequently interlinked challenges in the modern world. As rates of societal change increase, so does the operational tempo of police work (Sharps, 2022, 2024). Even venerable law enforcement challenges, such as public disorder, have acquired new dimensions, as recently observed in “social media-fueled” takeovers, such as that over the July 4, 2026 weekend in Newport Beach, California. In that situation, law enforcement deployed mounted officers. Horses are often very effective in police work; they can go where vehicles frequently can’t, and they provide psychological intimidation and sheer mass. However, the aftermath of the operations of mounted officers, in the media-intensive world of modern sensitivities, can be devastating for officers and department reputations alike. It’s a difficult call for police commanders to make.

It’s important to understand the psychology involved in choosing whether to use an older tactic in a novel social environment. The use of horses in harm's way has a long history, of course, and frequent sense; yet it’s proved difficult to give up even when using the horses was a very bad idea. For example, even in the twentieth century, some army officers fought the replacement of horses with mechanized armor with adamantine conviction. The last American horse cavalry charge actually occurred in World War II (Ramsey and Rivele, 1990). These operations in the twentieth century involved great courage, and were sometimes effective, as horse cavalrymen found new and unorthodox ways to fight. Yet superannuated horse-cavalry tactics in twentieth-century wars frequently resulted in insupportable casualty rates; and even so, some armies continued to drag horses up against machine guns and howitzers as if a battlefield full of Panzers was still the medieval mud of Agincourt. Why?

We Persist in Outdated Tactics

Even when conditions change, humans tend to persist in behaviors directed by prior mental sets, habits of mind which are very hard to break. As we continue to use these mental habits, we develop strong emotional investments in them, resulting in rigid thinking. We experience rigidity when we are not psychologically flexible. This can result from a strongly held belief that does not correspond with our perception of reality; in this case, belief in the value of horse cavalry when reality indicates otherwise. We may attempt to resolve faulty thinking by overvaluing an initial belief (Kashdan, 2010). This effect becomes particularly strong if we share the belief with others. We tend to conform to the opinions of others, especially to the opinions of people high in status; perhaps we've spent a few years in a cavalry regiment, surrounded by officers of high status who value horses beyond their actual current utility, and we’ve consequently invested our emotions in the mental sets involved, the combined effects of our psychological inflexibility and mental sets can become so profound that we do things which no longer make sense in the face of changing circumstances. These processes, in twentieth-century wars, caused armies to deploy horse cavalry under conditions that resulted in horrifying human casualties, to say nothing of losses among the poor, uncomprehending animals.

article continues after advertisement

In the world of strategy and tactics, the forces of mental sets are by no means confined to long-suffering horses. At its outset, World War I was expected to be a short conflict, and it might have been shorter if the powers involved had deployed their best firepower on the modern battlefield of the day, forcing negotiation rather than extended, unprecedented slaughter. Yet at the beginning of this truly terrible conflict, the Russian minister for war scolded his staff college for their interest in using firepower at all; he believed that this truly mechanized war would be won with the saber, the lance, and the bayonet charge. Incidentally, he also bragged that he had not read a military manual for the previous 25 years (Tuchman, 1962).

Not surprisingly, firepower won out. Heavy German artillery inflicted terrible casualties. The only way for the Allies to oppose such artillery was with very heavy artillery of their own. Yet, said a French officer, “Thank God we don’t have any!” (Tuchman, 1962). Many officers instead favored the maneuverability and higher firing rate of the vastly lighter French 75mm gun; a fine weapon, but it was massively outranged by German artillery. This mental set, together with massive German munitions, contributed to heavy casualties.

A Resistance to Change

The interaction of psychology with cannons has been a problem for a long time. Early in the nineteenth century, the best cannons were made of bronze. However, in the mid-nineteenth century, the Krupp industrial empire began to build them out of steel. They demonstrated one of these steel monsters to the Russian artillerists of Tsar Alexander II. After 4000 test rounds, the steel gun proved more durable, accurate, and powerful than any equivalent bronze weapon ever created.

The Russian officers were impressed. They were so impressed that they immediately added the steel demonstration weapon to the Artillery Museum of the Fortress of Peter and Paul, and continued with business as usual with bronze guns for decades to come (Manchester, 1964).

The psychology of strategy and tactics in military history is highly relevant to law enforcement; operational decisions made by commanders rely on the same basic psychological thinking processes in every situation. (Sharps, 2022, 2024). Although it is clearly not the place for psychologists to interfere in operational realms, it may be useful for law enforcement and other commanders to be very much aware of the psychological principles, as well as the tactical realities, that have driven important military and police decisions across contexts for centuries. Given the accelerating operational tempo of the modern world, we might therefore bear in mind Lord Salisbury’s political quote concerning “the commonest error…sticking to the carcasses of dead policies” (Steele, 1999). We’ve had the same human brains throughout history, but we can use our modern psychological knowledge to improve our decisions in today's world.
